utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Madam registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present, all the Defence teams are present, and today it's Mr. McCloskey on his own. The US government representative, Ms. Schildge, is also present. Good morning to you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. What are your travel arrangements, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about travel; but certainly with respect to scheduling, I have, in fact, checked and my schedule is clear for me to be available for the Court here through Friday, the 1st of February. If it is anticipated I'll be here beyond that, I will have to make some additional arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I hope we won't keep you that long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So does my wife, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So, in the meantime, I do encourage you to cut down on your cross-examination as much as you can, please. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in the meantime, via the Registry, I forwarded the translation of the document that was missing yesterday, and I also provided hard copies for both the Prosecution and the Bench as well, as well as for you. And I believe you were able to go through it in the meantime. My question will not go to the contents of the conversations mentioned, which take the most part of the document. My question, rather, refers to the chronology. You saw the intercepts being in chronological order between pages 3 or 4 until the end of the document. Did you notice that between the 12th and the 19th of July, there is not a single intercept that would be in that document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There's not a single intercept with respect to the actual text of them. Some of the material in these documents appear to be analytical abstracts of that material, but, for example, there's no verbatim text, as we're accustomed to seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, those pieces of text refer to a particular date; that is clear from the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Some of them refer to dates. Some of them refer to events that are happening on the ground that, when you look at the context of the statement, it's clear where it originated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the first paragraph of the first page again. Did you notice that there, the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina state that all of the tapes they had in their possession, referring to the events, they forwarded to the Agency for Research and Documentation back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct. And to further clarify, now that I've read this document in English, I can tell you that I have seen it at an earlier date, probably around 1997, 1998. So I can confirm now that I did have access and I did see this document at the early part of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My last question pertaining to this document is this: Did this raise any doubts, this fact that the AID has not been forwarding any tapes to you since 1995; although, they had them in their custody?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, this, among other information, was, in part, why I was prepared fully to not accept the broader body of intercepts at face value until the work of the OTP could independently corroborate them. This is just one of the many reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have a look at some specific intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I'd like to go to Exhibit P1144.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go through the text for yourself and tell me when you're done so that I can put the question to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on this intercept, do you conclude that one of the participants, and this is the only audible participant, is looking from the other collocutor a list of those suspected of having committed war crimes in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is the apparent thrust of the intercept, that the individual named "Zile" is doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see, from this intercept, that the request was being made so that those war crime suspects would be prevented from fleeing, as we can see from the text itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it's necessarily fleeing, but it certainly implies so there won't be a loss of near misses with respect to whether it's fleeing or whether it's the screening process. I see, and I also take your point, up in the beginning, "We'll miss them and they'll get away scott free." You can read that as fleeing, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to draw any conclusions, from the context of this intercept, as to the participants in the conversation, and them not knowing of any existence of a plan to execute all Muslim men which had surrendered or which had been captured from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that when I testified with respect to this intercept before, my interpretation was that the individual going under the name of "Zile," you know, believes that there is still going to be a screening process and that they're looking for information to support that, and that this particular individual is not aware at this time that there will, in fact, be no screening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were able to see lists of many members of the VRS and the Ministry of the Interior, and you were also able to identify some of them, could you draw any conclusions from this intercept as to who the person under the nickname of "Zile" is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've noted prior that I believe the individual named "Zile" is General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this particular intercept, we can see the time, which is 1829 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what date it was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Offhand, I don't recall whether this is dated -- has been dated as the 12th or the 13th of July. Memory is escaping me right now on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Our information states that the conversation happened on the 13th of July, but I presume you cannot recall the date correctly, and I won't insist on you doing so. Let us move on to the intercepts pertaining to my client, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at P1189A and C. First of all, let us go to page 2, line 3, since there is a technical error in the transcript of the conversation; that is, the name is spelled incorrectly. It is page 20005, line 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The name stated there is "Rocevic." However, if we look at line 3 of this intercept and of this page, perhaps you can confirm for us that the name appearing there is "Rosevic."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given my poor command of the language, I would probably be the last person you would want to ask that question of. I will certainly defer to your pronunciation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The name appearing in the third line is "Rosevic"; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not "Rocevic"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in the name of the town, correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are quite familiar with this intercept, since it was referred to on several occasions; therefore, there's no need to go through the whole of it. But on the face of it, it seems that it was intercepted at 1358; that is, two minutes before 2.00 p.m.. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's what it says on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on this intercept, you testified here that your conclusion was that a request was being made for 500 litres of fuel and that it might have to do with the transport of those captured at the school building at Kula to the Branjevo Farm, where they were subsequently executed. That was your testimony, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a military analyst and expert, can you confirm that for you to draw that conclusion, it is of great importance for you to know at what time the executions at Branjevo actually took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's -- the context around what happened in that entire village area of Pilica and the timing of that would be important, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information, and it is based on a testimony of one of the participants of the shooting at Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 10972, line 21 of the 4th of May, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He said that the executions at Branjevo began at 10.00 a.m. and were completed at 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. that day. Were you familiar with that information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's consistent with the testimony, as I understand, that Drazen Erdemovic gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this intercept that was intercepted just prior to 2.00, my conclusion is that the process of executions had been completed by that time. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, you've just told me, you know, going back to Mr. Erdemovic's testimony, that they were completed at 4.00 p.m. You're showing me an intercept that's at 2.00, so obviously they're not completed at this point, if one believes Mr. Erdemovic. And, further, I would note that while the intercept itself is dated as being intercepted at 1358 hours, we don't know at what juncture Colonel Popovic, at that location, actually asked for the fuel. So, no, I don't agree with your conclusion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic said that the executions were completed between 3.00 and 4.00, not at 4.00 p.m. But if the time you chose suits you best, then I have no objection to that. Another thing --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will even use your time at 1500. We'll use the earlier time. My conclusion remains the same. I don't think the 60 minutes makes a difference for why I've concluded what I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In order for you to make that conclusion, is the distance between the school at Kula and the Branjevo Farm of any relevance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it is unimportant whether we are talking about three or 100 or 200 kilometres; is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I'm saying is that the distance, the relevant portion for me, as part of my analysis and placing Colonel Popovic in the crime scene, is -- you know, has nothing to do with the relevant distance. What it has to do with is the actual context of the activity that he's involved in. Whether Colonel Popovic needs 500 litres of fuel because of distance or because of other variables, you know, I have no way of knowing whether he needs it or not. But for the context of my analysis, this document, you know, places and puts Colonel Popovic involved in that execution process in some manner. That was the relevant part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you draw your conclusion on his participation from this intercept; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, not totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have some additional sources of information that we don't? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In fact, the very next exhibit that I was shown by the Prosecutor with respect to this intercept was, in fact, the fuel dispersal log, which is not only a document that tends to heavily validate the authenticity of this particular intercept, but again in its own right reflects the fact that there is a specific request by Colonel Popovic for fuel. So, again, in part this, in part that particular fuel document, in part other evidence of intercepts and documents, and references within the IKM log of the Zvornik Brigade that show Colonel Popovic in that particular region on this day. Based on all of that information, that's what I draw my conclusion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly put, based on that, you concluded that the fuel mentioned was used to transfer the captured from the school to Branjevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know that the fuel was used primarily for that. I can't tell you that that fuel wasn't held up there and then the next day used for the burial operation, and I'm sure some of it may well have been, because the fuel ultimately wasn't returned -- or the remainder of the fuel wasn't returned back to Standard until later on the 17th. What I can tell you is that based on my analysis of all of the other activities that were happening or were not happening in Pilica on that day, particularly with respect to military operations, that that is the -- the use of that fuel, in part, for the conduct of the crime, you know, is the most logical explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at another intercept. It is 1D692. It is Intercept 662.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that we do not have it translated, and I will read it out for you. It is rather brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the top of the page so as to see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This conversation was intercepted on the 16th of July, 1995, by the SDB in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go down to the Intercept 662 itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "On the day mentioned, monitoring the RR axis of Zvornik-Vlasenica, at 7.85 megahertz frequency, Channel 9 at 1355, we registered a conversation between two unidentified males, X and Y." The conversation went as follows: X: "90 litres, 100 litres now." Y: "Fuck it." X: "We did our math on the map. 200 kilometres one way and two back. I don't know. What did you decide?" Y: "I don't know. I thought of going via Kotromanjica." X: "Where is that?" Y: "It's there, Dobrun Grada." X: "That's the direction?" Y: "Yes. Vito is going there, and he's going to stay in Uzice for 15 days." X: "I don't have that much fuel. Well, I don't know, I was thinking of telling that guy that he should give us some, and then when we are going to return, to know where to go." Y: "Well, if I am going to have any problems, then we should forward the old one. I'm not sure that's so far away." X: "Of course it is. I was looking at the map with one of the people from the traffic section. I'll see with my people whether I can secure that fuel; and if I do, we'll go together." Y: "I only called you to tell you." X: "It goes further by some 450 kilometres." Mr. Butler, have you seen this intercept before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The requested quantity of fuel, namely, 500 litres, plus one bus with a tank full of fuel, does this quantity tell you that the transport required ought to cover larger distances?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not really following the logical path of what you're asking. I have no idea if this particular intercept that you have read to me has any relation to what we're talking about. I mean, are you attempting to use it to illustrate how much fuel or how far a bus -- one bus should go, if that's, in fact, what we're talking about? I mean, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not my intention to tell you why I'm putting a question to you. Merely answer my question, if you can. My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. He's telling you, "Your question, I can't see clear," and you ought to either repeat your question in a different manner that is intelligible for your witness, or else you move to your next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear. You said that you haven't seen this intercept before, and I'm not asking you to analyse it. I'm going back to the intercept you did see, and I will later on go back to the document requesting 500 litres of fuel plus a bus with a tank full of fuel. As a military expert and analyst, does this not lead you to conclude that such a large quantity of fuel would be used for long-distance travel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Now I see where you're going. As was the practice of the VRS, they would only provide enough fuel that a particular vehicle or a particular mission required to prevent that fuel from being siphoned off for non-military reasons. I guess one conclusion that you can draw, if I guess this is where you're trying to go, is that you wouldn't issue that much particular fuel unless you were planning to go a particularly long distance. I mean, I assume that's what you're trying to get through the illustrative point of this intercept. I mean, that's one interpretation. Within the context of what we have been talking about, I don't think that that's the particular interpretation I would give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm or can you tell what the distance is between the Kula school and Branjevo, where the executions took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have personally never been up to that particular area. I have seen it on a map. I think we're talking about a distance of between five and ten kilometres, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the distance is far less, and I'm sure you know that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's argumentative and unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm certain of, and what I'm inviting you to tell me, is can you link up the quantity of fuel requested with the short-distance travel involving one or two buses holding prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That -- that hypothetical does not reflect the facts on the ground, and, as such, is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic. If we need to discuss this any further, it will have to be in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no. It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next issue I'd like to ask you about is the order for fuel which you looked at, which is Prosecution Exhibit number--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Zivanovic please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you kindly repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the bottom of the document, the end of the document, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please not broadcast the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom right corner of the document, there's a name of an individual, stating that he received the fuel concerned. Do you know if that individual was a member of the Command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which name are we talking about, sir? If -- there are two names I see at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is only one name in the bottom right-hand corner and a signature.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So we're talking -- oh, yes. No. I don't know offhand if that individual is a member of the Drina Corps or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever come to know who the individual is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't believe I've personally looked at who that individual is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about this individual from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that I did. I mean, I'm not aware of this particular individual at all. I mean, I assume he's a member of the Zvornik Brigade, but I don't know that as a fact, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't go looking for it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't go interview this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that nowhere in this document can the signature of Vujadin Popovic be found?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a working knowledge of what his signature looks like, so I can't confirm or deny that. I don't know. I mean, I don't know if Colonel Popovic's signature is on this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the translation of the document, can you perhaps find his signature or any other signature that is unclear or illegible to you in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I mean, I see his name listed. I don't see a signature listed with him. I mean, if you're telling me that he didn't sign this document, I will have no reason to doubt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want you to believe anything I say. I just want you to look at the document and tell me if you see that signature or a place where the signature should be put. If you don't know, that's fine. I won't insist.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. All I can tell you is I see his name written down there in handwriting. I don't see anything which I would purport to be his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to go back to the earlier document; namely, 1189. That's an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at the time the conversation took place, from Vlasenica to Zvornik, the quantity of two tonnes of fuel was being dispatched? Can this be concluded on the basis of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll down on the English language version?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's on page 2, but you can go through the entire intercept if that's easier.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what you're referring to is at the bottom of page 1, sir, and it is a reference there, after, "Don't you have 500 litres of oil?" The next sentence is: "They're asking for two tonnes loaded." I can't make that conclusion, only because the next sentence says, from the Palma duty officer, "Well, I don't know." The Palma duty officer is certainly not aware that there is already two tonnes of fuel coming up to Zvornik. Whether other members of the Rear Services Branch know or not is unclear, so I don't know the answer to that. I can't say that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to the other document; namely, 1201, another intercept, and I'm interested in the items A and C.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation between Popovic, himself, and Rasic. It was on the basis of this conversation that you concluded, on the basis of his words, that he had finished his business. You concluded that he was referring to him having finished the executions or completed the executions. Is that -- was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, that's what I believe the testimony -- that's what my testimony was concerning one portion of the intercept. The first portion of the intercept, I believe Colonel Popovic is talking about the fact that he was up with Pandurevic. He has discussed issues related to the column with Pandurevic, and he's referring to Colonel Pandurevic's interim combat report of 16 July. I think the second part, where we start into, you know: "... I finished the job." "You finished?" "I finished everything." "Good." "I'll come there tomorrow when I'm sure that it's all been taken care of." That, I conclude he's now talking about the murder operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the function held by Vujadin Popovic at the time, do you find his -- that his stay in Zvornik may have been related to the affairs that fell within his purview under the rules?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The implication that there's an ongoing counter-intelligence mission that requires his presence there? I'm not aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to other matters.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other matters that he might be conducting, you know, within the context of the legal prosecution of his rules, you know, his purpose being there was to facilitate the murder operation. The fact that he was there and that General Krstic sent him out as the nearest Drina Corps staff officer to find out personally from Colonel Pandurevic what was happening and why is certainly within his competence to do. I'm not aware of any other mission that he is performing that would be strictly related to his counter-intelligence role as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that at the time, the column which was retreating from Srebrenica was posing a threat to Zvornik; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 13th and -- you know, the 12th and 13th, from where the column was moving up, it did pose a threat particularly to the town of Zvornik. By 16 July, it was evidently clear to everybody, to include Colonel Pandurevic, that there was no military threat to the town of Zvornik at that time. The threat was to the military units in the front lines, and that was the predication for letting the column through. So, you know, Zvornik is a large municipality. If we're talking about Zvornik town, the threat is greatest on the evening of 12/13 July, when the column would have had the ability to attack the town. That threat didn't exist by the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my understanding of where the column would have been the morning and afternoon of 14 July, I would say that there would be an outside possibility that they could have switched their direction and attacked Zvornik proper; but at that point, as far as the column was advancing in the other direction, it would have been a very, very difficult military task to do, probably beyond their ability. But, you know, in the abstract, I will grant them that they had that capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your estimate, the column was even farther away on the 15th and was an even less a threat to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Zvornik, correct. Conversely, since the army was deployed west of the town, along the confrontation lines, that raised the military threat to the Zvornik Brigade military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that mobilisation was declared in Zvornik. You probably can't recall when this occurred, in light of the earlier dates, the other dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll show another document, which is 698. It's in e-court. We have the translation as well. This isn't the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This isn't the document I was asking for, but I have a hard copy and I'll ask you to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the B/C/S version. I don't know if it's possible to place both versions at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the request sent by the commander of the Drina Corps, General Krstic, for non-assigned conscripts to be mobilised, and the date is the 15th of July. I don't know if you've had time to look at it, but tell me, it arises from this that mobilisation was ordered on the 15th of July, or rather, this is a piece of evidence that mobilisation was sought on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document here ordering it, which is document 697, and I don't think it's in the system either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It arises from this that on the 15th of July, mobilisation was ordered in Zvornik, and it's on this basis that I conclude that there was a threat to Zvornik. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I believe the key phrase in these particular documents are "those conscripts that have not been assigned to the war formations." As you will note, there was an earlier mobilisation order, in some units as early as the 9th, as late as the 12th, which reflect the mobilisation of all individuals assigned to the Zvornik Brigade who might have otherwise been there. Certainly, the fact that they want to now mobilise even more individuals and have them report to the Zvornik Brigade reflects the military situation at the time and their understanding of it. Having said that, we also know, from the other information, exactly where the military threat is, because it's reflected by where Colonel Pandurevic is sending the units. They're not being sent to Zvornik town. They're in fact being sent to the area of Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I want to let you know that they are in e-court. You should put "1D" before the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] 1D697. It is a document of -- it is an order for mobilisation of -- a request for mobilisation of the Drina Corps commander. And 697 is order of Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't put "1D," so they could find it. They are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "1D," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the document in the system now as well. Do you see that the mobilisation was ordered with a view to securing the territory in the area of responsibility from infiltrated sabotage groups and broken-up Muslim groups from Srebrenica, as the text says? Is that what paragraph 1 of the order says?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are the security organs duty-bound, as part of their duties, to detect such groups through counter-intelligence methods?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the abstract, they are, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if security organs have any duties pertaining to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall a specific notation of that. However, given the broader responsibilities of the security branch, I could foresee a situation where, during particularly the initial screening of mobilisation, where they're getting information from potential conscripts, that there would be a reason to -- for security personnel to look over that to determine if any of the individuals might be potential security or counter-intelligence threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question: Since you had occasion to read a number of military rules applied in the VRS Army, did you have occasion to read the Rules of Mobilisation of the Armed Forces, called "PRAMOS," for short?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't believe that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, yesterday you took three hours and 31 minutes. Your time will -- of five hours will expire at 10.30, so you need to finish by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Yes, I'll do that. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will not be asking you, then, if you know whether the security organs carry out the so-called securing -- or providing security for mobilisation. Tell me, why is it that you did not consider the stay of Vujadin Popovic as the security organ in Zvornik as one required by his usual duties? Do you wish to state that he did not, in fact, perform his duties at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered the location of where Colonel Popovic was; but as you will note, on the basis of the intercepts and other information, Colonel Popovic wasn't in Zvornik on -- for most of the time on the 16th and 17th. He was, in fact, up in Pilica. Under your supposition that he's in Zvornik somehow shepherding the mobilisation, the conscripts are being mobilized at Standard and he's a dozen, 15, 20 kilometres to the north? I don't make the connection that you do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about his counter-intelligence work? Was he supposed to do that at Standard alone or in the field as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pandurevic [sic], by function and responsibility, could have performed his counter-intelligence mission anywhere that he deemed necessary. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Popovic," you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my apologies. Colonel Popovic. But, again, I have -- I have come across no information whatsoever that reflects a particular counter-intelligence threat that would have warranted his presence up in Pilica at the time in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your understanding, does counter-intelligence work or activity take place only in a location where there is an attack or any combat activity, or can it be performed at other locations as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, sir. It can be -- it can be performed wherever it needs to be performed. Counter-intelligence has no direct correlation to a particular military attack. It doesn't even have a direct correlation to an armed conflict. It occurs in peacetime as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree that it needn't take place or be linked to the same location where there is combat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe I just said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You testified here that the corridor at Baljkovica was opened on the 16th of July and that Popovic was issued with an order to go and see why that happened and to check whether it was done properly. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified that the information was that Colonel Popovic was directed to go out and find Colonel Pandurevic and get an explanation as to whether a corridor had been opened and why. I think it's a foregone conclusion that it wasn't done properly, because no one on the Drina Corps Main Staff had directed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown a note, I believe, from the duty officer's logbook, and it states there that he was to go there. Do you not understand that as an order that was given to him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe I've testified that he was -- he was directed to go there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the corridor was opened on the next day? It wasn't open and closed the same day, but it remained open for a period of about 24 hours or a bit longer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you link that to his words, when he said that he was going to come the next day when he will be certain that everything is fine? Did you understand that to mean that he was to wait until the corridor was closed and things completed so that he can submit his final report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't believe that that was the context that he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you think he wasn't supposed to do that or that he did not do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His original purpose up there, as I've indicated, was to facilitate the executions. He was drawn off of that original purpose by a direct order of the Drina Corps, presumably General Krstic personally, to find out what was going on with Colonel Pandurevic. Once Colonel Pandurevic either reported back to Colonel Popovic what had happened, and in conjunction he had written his interim combat report of that day, explaining in great detail what he did and why he did it, General Krstic had the answers that he'd needed. In context, obviously, so did the Main Staff, which resulted in the dispatch of a number of officers, on the morning of the 17th, from the Main Staff to inquire, themselves, what was going on. There's no information that I'm aware of that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was part of that inquiry process. So, if he wasn't out at Baljkovica, talking with Colonel Pandurevic and Major Obrenovic, and either with Colonel Stankovic, Colonel Turkulja, Colonel Sladoje -- let me pronounce that correctly, Sladojevic, I believe, the only other issue that was again occurring at that time was the burial operation of the bodies at the Branjevo Farm. So because I could not place him at the legitimate military activity, the information that I have, as well as other information, places him up at Pilica during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, having in mind Mr. Popovic's position and duties, can you explain, the way you see it as an expert, why was he supposed to be singled out to assist the executions and assist the burial of the corpses, rather than to perform his regular duties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of the large-scale crimes that were occurring - and I take it as, you know, that even they recognised at the time, at face value, it was a crime - there was a vested interest in making sure that evidence of that crime was appropriately covered up. That would require, in large part, you know, the ability to, you know, use military police, facilitate the use of engineers, things of that nature. The commanders obviously felt that the security officers would be the best individuals to either facilitate -- you know, to facilitate the executions as well as to ensure that there would be as little evidence around as possible after the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in your belief, such a complex operation could only be performed by person number 3 in the corps and that plain officers and soldiers could not do such a thing, such as burying corpses and checking whether they had been buried properly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I certainly hold open that possibility, and I believe that the activity at other crime scenes reflects the involvement of those individuals as well. This was not an activity that Colonel Popovic exclusively was in charge of or even did individually, but his role up there at that location was to facilitate the accomplishment of that particular mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion, again, points to the fact, and perhaps you can confirm this to us or not, that the duties that Popovic was supposed to perform, and the only ones he could - this being counter-intelligence, since he couldn't delegate those to anyone else - remained not taken care of, since he was delegated to do other things. Can you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what counter-intelligence tasks he was involved in at that particular time, so I don't know whether or not they were being taken care of or not. I just don't have an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the mobilisation order, you saw that there was mobilisation precisely because of the terrorist groups that had been infiltrated, and counter-intelligence was there to locate and gather knowledge about those groups. In your words, Popovic was not engaged in that, since he was busy burying corpses, in your words. Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- yes. It's my assertion; although, I just -- I still don't understand the connection that, you know, the activity that was occurring in the Zvornik Brigade zone of identifying these small groups of Muslims who were either trapped behind the lines or things of that nature, how that's a classic counter-intelligence function. Colonel Popovic, you know, isn't beating the bushes, you know, with operative sources looking for these individuals, and certainly interviewing recently-mobilised conscripts isn't going to get him any answers, either, as to where these people are located. So I'm just not sure how a task that is defined as strictly a counter-intelligence task is assisting the military situation at hand at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From your answer, I conclude that detecting sabotage groups is one of the tasks under the remit of security organs, and they have their own counter-intelligence measures for that. Do you stand by that, since I never said that security organs set up ambushes or fight the groups?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, but - and, certainly, I didn't mean to make the case that you did - what I'm saying is that the Drina Corps and particularly the Zvornik Brigade at that time, you know, despite what they were labelled in this particular mobilisation order, you know, knew that the military threat was not what we would call a sabotage and terrorist group infiltrating the lines in order to conduct a specific act of sabotage or terrorist in an area. What the military threat was is dozens of groups who had been separated from the main body of the column, many of them who were armed, many who were presumably lost, who were wandering around the zone -- or the rear areas of the zone of Zvornik Brigade and, as such, posed a potential military threat. You know, as I indicated earlier, in -- given that that's the context of the military threat, you know, I'm not aware how the classical functions of a counter-intelligence officer assists in a military commander getting a better handle on what that threat is and dealing with it. The only way that that particular officer would be able to provide any information of relevance to someone like Colonel Pandurevic or Major Obrenovic would be following the capture of individuals and their interrogation in order to provide information from those individuals as to the sizes and locations of other units of stragglers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you stating that such matters cannot be ascertained via the network of cooperatives that security organs usually have in place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a situation where there was a source of information that may have come from a cooperative at 2nd Corps or things of that nature on a specific sabotage group, I concede that would have been a likely function, but that wasn't the situation facing the Zvornik Brigade on that particular day or the next. They didn't -- the VRS didn't have operatives with those straggler groups, collecting information on their intentions and things of that nature. What they had, in fact, was, through their radio intercepts, through interviews with captured prisoners, as well as, you know, in the case of Colonel Pandurevic, the negotiations with Semso Muminovic - I hope I pronounced his name correctly - Colonel Pandurevic had a fairly good reading of what the military objective of the column was in that context. So, I mean, I agree with your point, exactly what counter-intelligence people can do; but in the context of the time and the threat that we're talking about here, they weren't doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you exclude the possibility that the security organs were busying themselves with their counter-intelligence tasks whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I never exclude possibilities, but I have no information whatsoever which supports that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree that such information is otherwise confidential and they are not made public?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I would agree and remind you that we're sitting on approximately 350.000 VRS documents that are also confidential and state secret that are not otherwise made public. That goes for all military documents; and in those documents, there are some security-related material. I mean, there -- again, we never exclude a possibility analytically, certainly I don't, but there's just no evidence to support that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a general question concerning the intercepts you referred to. You noticed that in certain places in those conversations, dots appear. We were given information that if a part of a conversation was inaudible, such dots would appear. That was the explanation given by the operators. When interpreting such intercepts, how did you interpret such dots, in other words, the parts of those conversations which remained inaudible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same way you did, sir. I mean, my understanding of the dots was either that parts of the conversation were either inaudible or that there was an indeterminate time delay where there was silence or something else and then the conversation picked up again. I mean, that's how I understand that those symbols are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that those dots might be there to mark a period of time, for example, a moment of pause in a conversation, when the collocutor are not saying anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've heard that once or twice, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The words that are missing and the words that we have dots appearing instead for, can they change the thrust of a conversation, give it a different direction or mean something that could influence your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, sir, words that are either unintelligible or otherwise not included in intercepts certainly could change the context by which I would read that intercept or read it for a specific piece of information. I mean, as a matter of doing any form of analysis, you'd like as much complete information -- you know, you'd like to get the complete story behind it, the complete set of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, just one more question: You were the Prosecution's expert in this case, which is completely fine; but to say it outright, I am one of the people who doubted your objectivity, since I believe that your close ties with the Prosecution and the investigation, as you took part of to a significant degree, compromised your objectivity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey didn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Everything is fine except the personalising of it, his view of it. It's just not appropriate; it's never relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, but Mr. Zivanovic, I'm sure, will appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] This is my last question, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I could gather that. I could gather that, but go straight to it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: In your opinion, the close ties I just referred to, did they have any impact on the objectivity of your conclusions in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I am human, so I'm not going to tell you that I don't have human characteristics, despite what some people will say about me. As an analyst, I recognise there are dangers of bias creeping in. As to my close ties, my close personal ties with these people, I would also remind you that, you know, as a career military intelligence officer in my own army, I have very close ties to the success or failure of the United States Army. That doesn't mean that in serving my commanders, I serve them best by slanting information to the way they want to hear it. I am trained by profession to, as much as I possibly can, provide the information in as accurate a form as possible, because that's how I best serve the people who are in leadership positions over me. Sometimes that means telling them things that they don't want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Those are my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler can leave the courtroom, and we'll have the break. In the meantime, Mr. Haynes, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Zivanovic; Mr. Zivanovic is the least concerned, even though this document is a"1D" document. Earlier on in the day, Mr. Haynes and Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Zivanovic made available the English translation of the document he made use of yesterday, and I'm talking of 1D221. You will recall he asked the witness whether he would agree that there were no intercepts between the 12th and the 19th of July of 1995. It's not that that I am referring to. But under the entry of the 19th of July, 1995, page 7 in the English version, we'd like you to look at the translation, Mr. Haynes and Mr. McCloskey. We only want to know whether you agree that the translation is a correct translation, and that's it. We don't want any further comments. We just want to make sure that this is a correct translation of the original, and you can come to us at your convenience later on. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who's next? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, my name is John Ostojic, and I represent Ljubisa Beara. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to start by -- where my learned friend left off, and that is with your curriculum vitae; and in reviewing that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for the Court, it's 65 ter 681 on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I note, in your educational background that you provide for us, that you have no law enforcement education. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which version you're looking at. I believe one of them should -- that particular document, 2007, should reflect the education at the Law Enforcement Centre in Glencoe, Georgia, where as an intelligence professional now with law enforcement, I was required to attend a six-week course. I believe that will be on page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least on the page that we have on the monitor, the third paragraph under "Professional Background," is "Six years of combined military and criminal analytical ..." I was reading --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. "Six years of combined military and criminal analytical intelligence support for international prosecutors and related law enforcement professionals, conducting investigations into violations," et cetera. Is that what you mean, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. That reflects my work here. What I'm specifically referring to I believe is on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's page 4, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it page 4? Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's go to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question, though, is: This was a training course, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, a basic intelligence training course. It was a six-week course at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking specifically about your period prior to the time that you came to work for the ICTY and the OTP. Prior to that, you had no education, no background, whatsoever, in law enforcement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And prior to coming to work for the OTP, you also had no criminal law education, to speak of; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's stay with this page 4 for a moment. And you list three training courses or seminars that you attended, including the one where you received the technical certificate, a technical certification course. Can you tell me how long -- you told us the first one in 2004 was a six-week course. The one in 1997, how long was this advanced course that you took in Arizona?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The course is structured into two components. The first component was roughly an 18-month curriculum that was a non-resident part. The actual attendance part was a six-week curriculum.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what about with respect to the 1988 course where you received a technical certification course, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just a six-week residence course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, now that we know that you had no law enforcement or criminal law experience -- strike that. Now that we know that you had no law enforcement education and no criminal law education prior to coming to the OTP, let's turn to your experience, sir. Am I also correct that prior to coming to work for the OTP, you did not have any law enforcement experience or criminal law experience?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And on January 14th, when you first started testifying here - on page 28, line 10 from my learned friends - you said something to the effect as follows, quote, that you "learned techniques and tactics" while you were dealing with law enforcement in your position with the OTP. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me what those techniques and tactics were that you learned with respect to dealing with law enforcement, since you had no education and experience in those areas prior to that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by virtue of having access to not only a world-class body of lawyers, but also investigators from both common law and civil law backgrounds, what I was able to do is, by watching them work, looking at what they were doing and what they were trying to accomplish with respect to their own investigations, it gave me the foundation to be able to look at what types of military information they would need to support their investigative process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I honestly don't know if I understand you. Was that a technique or a tactic that you explained to me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a combination of both.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, list out any other technique, if you will, that you learned relating to law enforcement while you were with the OTP, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one technique I would use, and I still use today, is a technique that many civil law investigators use, where, in an interview, even if they believe that the subject is not providing accurate information or is misrepresenting them, rather than initially confronting the individual, they will allow the interview to go through an entire statement, from beginning to end, and only at that juncture will they intervene to ask specific questions. Conversely, many of the particularly American and Canadian and Australian investigators would not take that approach and would, in fact, as soon as it became clear to them, they would intervene in an attempt to get the individual who they were interviewing to give information that they believe was more truthful. So, I mean, that is an example of a technique that I learned while here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about a tactic? Share with me a tactic that you may have learned.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tactic with respect to law enforcement that we would often use is that when we set up a particular interview mission, looking to confirm or deny specific facts, what we would often do is structure the targets that we were interviewing to start with the lowest-ranking person first in order to establish not only what their own personal activities were during a relevant period, but also to give us information as to what their superiors were doing. So we would take that particular tactic into account, so that when we finally got to the point where we were interviewing the superior, you know, by virtue of earlier interviews, we felt that we had a good idea what this individual's activities were during a relevant period. So that's how I would define it as a tactic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to working with the OTP, am I correct that you were never involved in a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. As a US Army intelligence officer, I'm forbidden by law to have been involved in criminal investigations in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And prior to working with the OTP, am I correct that you never authored a report with respect to your analysis to be used in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To be used in a court of law, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or to be published anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have authored a number of classified reports that were published that are not in courts of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to working with the OTP, sir, am I correct that you were never retained or requested to be a witness in a local, national, or international criminal proceeding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So the only experience you have with respect to testifying would, in fact, be when it started here with the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about -- we discussed independence or you were kind enough to say you were human, as we all can see, and that you may have certain biases. Do you agree with me, sir, that you're not an independent outsider?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And would you also agree with me that you're not independent, per se?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That entirely depends on how you define "per se."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at your testimony in the Blagojevic case, pages 4755, lines 13 through 18, where you say, quote, you are not "independent, per se," end quote. Why don't you tell me, sir, what you mean by "per se."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I am not independent insomuch as I work for the Office of the Prosecutor; and in that context, the material that I am reviewing for the most part is within the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. I am independent insomuch as the purpose, the focus and the conclusions of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that shortly, I'm sure. And you also describe yourself, sir, as being an integrated member of the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was an integrated member of the investigative team. If I said "OTP," I certainly mean within the Srebrenica team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you also describe yourself not only as being integrated but as a strategic member of the OTP, do you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the Srebrenica team and investigation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Butler, could you slow down a little bit and allow a short pause between question and answer for the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Mr. Butler. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk a little bit about bias. With respect to bias, will you agree with me that one issue, analytically speaking, that remains out there is the fact that there is a bias in one direction or another, and it's because there may be a lack of information that an analyst may look at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bias is generally -- with respect to internal factors, I don't view bias as an issue of a lack of information. That's a completeness issue. A lack of information can lead to potentially a biased conclusion. So, I mean, in that context, I agree with what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic. Let's cut through this in a radical way. You're here as an expert witness brought forward by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you understand your role or what do you understand your role to be now, as an expert, Prosecution expert witness, vis a vis the Trial Chamber and parties in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, as I've always understood my role when testifying before this Chamber and prior Chambers, I am a witness at the disposal of the Court, not for the Prosecutor, not for the Defence, but to provide whatever information that the Court deems necessary to make its decision. I'm not going to say I'm an independent arbitrator of facts, such as an expert who's had no association with the Office of the Prosecutor could say, but I believe that the way my reports are written and my information is provided, that I am being as fair and as technically accurate as I can for the assistance of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And with all due respect to Mr. President and Your Honours, I do not believe you are an expert, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me read what you said in Blagojevic on November 17th, 2003, on page 4692, lines 2 through 9. Here's what you say when you were asked by Defence counsel there: "Well, Mr. Karnavas, with respect to my own personal feelings and opinions, I try to keep them out as much as possible. However, with respect to bias, the one issue, analytically speaking, that remains out there is the fact that as -- myself personally, as an analyst, and all analysts engaged in this field, we are limited to the amounts and types of information that we have available to us at the time. So if there is, in fact, a bias in one direction or another, it may very well be in fact because of lack of information." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe I've said earlier that a lack of information can, in fact, lead -- you know, is a cause of bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at some information that you may not have examined in evaluating and in preparing your report, if you don't mind. Did you, sir, at any time review or request intercepts that may have been received from other countries or taken by other countries for the period in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the investigative team did request that information, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you list for me the countries that they requested that information from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're getting into the area of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'd like to be heard specifically on that point, but perhaps outside the presence of the witness. Also, I would add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- when we addressed this issue before, at the beginning of the case with another witness, the Court instructed me not to go further with those questions because a representative from the United States government was not present, and we complied. We're grateful, and we do have a representative from the United States government here, so I'm sure that she can protect the interests, if it even borders on a Rule 70 issue, which I don't believe that it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you are jumping to the conclusion that the information was drawn from the US government, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, and that would be Rule 70 protected. And I can tell you that there's many countries involved here; and the US, whether they are a country or not, is not an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I wouldn't like to proceed with this discussion in the presence of the witness. So if you are going to make further submissions, then the witness must leave the courtroom, and then we'll see. I think you can safely move to your next question, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I'd like to be heard, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So should I wait or should the Court invite the witness to leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I've already said that if you want to discuss this further, the witness must leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would like to discuss it further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the witness must leave the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This witness, in prior testimony, specifically identifies that there were intercepts from other countries, and he says that they were from many other countries, and he identifies one country being the United States. So I don't know at that time why there wasn't an objection. There was not. I consider it to be waived at this point. Nevertheless, since we do have counsel from the United States government, we'd like to hear from her on that issue. But I don't believe that Rule 70 extends to the other countries as well. We know and believe that there were other countries who were trying to and did obtain intercept information that would be exculpatory. We need to know when they were requested by the Office of the Prosecution, if they received those intercepts, in order for the Court to get the complete picture with respect to what the Prosecution has only offered evidence of one side; namely, the ABiH intercept operators. I can tell the Court I believe, it's my understanding, based on understanding and belief, that the Croatian government also was conducting intercept operations and have, from articles that we've seen from time to time, suggested that they do have intercept material in connection with July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Regarding Croatia, Mr. President, we have provided intercept material related to the Croatian government that's nothing to do with Rule 70, and that is part of the information provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and if -- I would like to be directed to where Mr. Butler has mentioned US intercepts in the past. I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, that I can't tell you. What I can remember vividly is that during his testimony here, he did hint or affirm that apart from the intercepts that we've been talking about here, the ones allegedly obtained or captured by the BiH, there were intercepts from other countries. That he did say, but he didn't specify the name of any source or country as a source of these intercepts. Anyway, let's hear what Mr. Bourgon has to say, and then we'll decide. Yes, Mr. Bourgon, in the meantime, if you can indicate to Mr. McCloskey where the witness alleged or mentioned the US as a source of information in relation to intercepts, please do so. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the Prosecution's objection at this time highlights a fundamental problem with the testimony of this witness. Mr. Butler was completely integrated into the Prosecution team. He has had access to everything that the Prosecution had access to. Today, he's testifying before you, and we want to say that even though he had access to information, whether substantive or information in the sense of who was contacted, he cannot be -- we cannot say that today he cannot disclose this information as part of his testimony or else his testimony will be incomplete. It's a fundamental problem. If the Prosecution elects to pick one of their own to testify before this Chamber, saying that he does not have a bias and that he is independent, he must be able to disclose all of the information in his possession. My colleague from the Prosecution should have requested the authorisation from any Rule 70 provider so that the testimony of Mr. Butler can be complete. If it cannot be complete, it should be stopped right now. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He cites no authority. There is none that suggests that because the witness takes the witness stand, Rule 70 disappears. Rule 70 is a crucial rule in order to obtain the assistance of governments, and it is a rule that we must support. Just going back in my memory regarding other intercepts, I think one of the things Mr. Butler, I believe, was referring to was the JNA or the VRS ability to take, to do intercepts and that they were intercepting as well. He made a reference to that. But as for countries beyond the former Yugoslavia, I'm not aware of any reference that has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think Mr. McCloskey, my learned friend, misunderstands our question. We support Rule 70 as well. However, once the Prosecution decides to call a witness, we believe that anything and everything he reviewed should be provided to the Defence and should be open for discussion during, at the very least, cross-examination. Now, the Court's ruling was rather specific when we questioned Mr. Ruez, that the absence of a United States government counsel restricted us from going further, and I believe my learned friend Mr. Bourgon is correct. This should have been anticipated, and I discussed it, quite frankly, with Mr. McCloskey, among other issues including aerial imagery, and I also discussed it with my learned friend with the United States government, that I would be asking these types of questions. They should be prepared now to share their position on that. Perhaps the United States government does not object to this question, and I would invite the Court to, if allowed, respectfully, to hear the position from the United States government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, before we get to that, your question didn't relate just to the United States government. Your question related to other countries, requiring the witness to then outline which other countries, which could include a vast array of countries, as far as we know. So I think it's a bit premature to get to the question of the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, I couldn't agree more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But I should not -- and thank you, Your Honour. I should not be prohibited in asking the question of what countries. If in fact there were more countries, then it's the obligation, I believe, of the Prosecution to get Rule 70 clearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think we are missing -- we are missing the most important point in this whole discussion; namely, if the Prosecution is telling you Mr. Butler, at the time he worked for the Prosecution, may have become privy to information and the sense that other countries outside the former Yugoslavia may have provided intercept information relating to the July 1995 events, does not mean that the witness now, who is a witness, an expert witness and no longer part of the Prosecution team, is free to divulge that information if he couldn't divulge it at the time he was working for the Prosecution because it was covered by Rule 70 privilege. This is the whole point.
