Does the fact that a witness who was part of the Prosecution and who ceases to be part of the Prosecution and becomes an expert witness here, even albeit a Prosecution expert witness, mean that he has no longer the obligation to keep Rule 70 protected evidence protected? This is the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I agree, Mr. President, and that's the very reason why his lawyer's in court today, and his lawyer from the United States government can take that position, if they so desire, that it's confidential and should remain confidential. But the Court, I should suggest, and certainly not the Prosecution, can make that ruling with respect to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we believe that you have exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Sorry for interrupting you like this, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We believe that the Trial Chamber has pinpointed the exact situation. If the witness has had access to information, information which is relevant to his expertise and information which he cannot disclose today, for whatever reason, Rule 70 or another reason, then the witness is not in the position to give a complete testimony in all fairness to the accused in this courtroom; and, therefore, his testimony should be stopped. If my colleague wants to put a witness on the stand who has worked before with the Office of the Prosecution, he should have obtained the necessary clearance for the witness to be able to answer these questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. McCloskey, and that will be the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before hearing from you: Mr. Bourgon, just a brief question. On your part, having known that the witness had access to whatever material, why did you not ask for the access to it beforehand, before the witness comes to the courtroom? Why did you not bring the attention of the Chamber to that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because the burden is not on us. We don't know what the witness is testifying about. We don't know what we will do, what we will cross-examine the witness on until we've heard examination-in-chief. It is not for the Defence, Judge, to identify the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That did not appear in the examination-in-chief, the intercepts, potential intercepts, by other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But one of the things the Defence will necessarily do, as part of cross-examination, is go to the sources that were used or that were available to the expert to make his testimony. If we have information of material that was used, it is normal for the Defence to take it for granted that the witness will be able to go back to these sources and talk about them. Today, we are surprised to hear that at the first question that is asked about some material, about some of the sources, by my colleague Mr. Ostojic, that we have an objection from the Prosecution saying the witness can't do that. It was for the Prosecution to seek the Rule 70 clearance if there is a Rule 70 issue. The Defence is not in a position to know whether there is a Rule 70 issue or not until it comes up. It is for the Prosecution. The burden is on the Prosecution to identify these issues and to make it sure that the witness will be able to give full and complete testimony in all fairness to the accused in this courtroom. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as Judge Kwon pointed out, we have not elicited from Mr. Butler anything to do with intercepts from any countries aside from the former Yugoslavia, and there is no law supporting this outrageous argument that it is incumbent upon us to seek Rule 70 clearance. There has been no suggestion by the Prosecution of any such thing in any country. This is a fishing expedition on whether or not even the United States has a dog in this fight, and we cannot assume, by calling on the United States, that they do. That would be, in itself, a Rule 70 violation. They're not here as Mr. Butler's personal lawyer. They're here to look after the interests of the United States, and I'm here to look after the interests of Rule 70 in this case. We have not used any such material. This door needs to remain closed. We can't fish on whether or not any country has provided us information that we're not relying on. It's just inappropriate and goes well beyond the scope of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon, I said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I add one short detail, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come on, and that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler is testifying because he was a former employee of the United Nations and the Office of the Prosecutor. Once the -- the day that he is called as a witness, it is fair for the Defence to assume that my colleague from the Prosecution has obtained the necessary clearance so that the testimony can be complete. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to make four points as briefly as I can. The first, I think, Mr. Bourgon has sought to make, and it's the answer to Judge Kwon's observation, is that the duty of disclosure, whether it be material supportive of their case or exculpatory of the case, is upon the Prosecution. The second point is this: I don't think anybody here contends that Mr. Butler today is not an OTP witness. If Mr. McCloskey wants to contend that, I will put before him an e-mail he sent me only a couple of weeks ago in which he used the phrase, "We all agree Butler has his OTP hat back on." He's an OTP witness, plain and simple. The third really goes to the substance of where we've got to. The point that Mr. Ostojic is seeking to make is a simple one, and I'm sure we're all following it. The point he's seeking to make is that conclusions that Mr. Butler has come to in his narrative are necessarily biased because he has ignored material that might have pointed him in a different direction. The objection that is made at this moment is premature. Mr. Ostojic has really not got past first base, to use an expression he'd understand. It is not the question that is protected by Rule 70, it's the material itself. There's really a three-stage process. Did the OTP ask for it? Did they get it? Where from? And what was it? And so far, all Mr. Ostojic has asked is, "Was it requested?" And I simply do not see how it can sensibly be contended that the answer to that question is in some way protected by Rule 70. It may be that Mr. Ostojic cannot go to base 2 or base 3. But to make his point that Mr. Butler's conclusions are biased because he has been blinkered to material or been denied material, to use the words he used in the Blagojevic case, the answer to this question is not protected by Rule 70 and can't be. Those are the submissions I make in support of Mr. Ostojic's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to add anything, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to join to the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just in brief response to his honoured QC from Mr. Pandurevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That is offensive, I'm sorry. That is offensive, and I want an apology for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In my knowledge, I thought I was paying you respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I don't believe you did think that for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought that was an appropriate title. I'm sorry if it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move. I can understand Mr. Haynes perfectly well, but it's probably the American approach, as distinct from the English approach. Two great countries divided by the same language, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will seek his guidance on the appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "Mr. Haynes" will do fine from now until the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually, we have the same problem between husband and wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: True. The question is: Question 1, on whether or not Mr. Butler has or the investigation has sought Rule 70 is not relevant, because question 2 can never be answered, because it must remain in secret if any country responded in any way, because that answer provides the kind of intelligence information that those countries do not want public. So the first question is not relevant because the second part can never be relevant. You've got to get to first base before you get to second base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ostojic, do you wish to add anything, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Certainly, I endorse what my learned friend Mr. Haynes said. But to just respond to what the OTP said earlier, when they say that the United States government doesn't have a dog in the fight and his analogy about fishing, really, if we look at the aerial images, we know that they've asked for them. They've produced them with no problems with respect to Rule 70. We were allowed to see that there were some differences, and I'm going to inquire of that of Mr. Butler, as learned friend knows, as does my friend from the United States government. So to suggest that is just not correct, and it's simply not true. We have a right to know this information. It is not our obligation to ask them every day for materials that witnesses have relied on. This Court has ordered it. The Rules of this Tribunal require it, and they've simply fail to abide by both these rules and the Court's order in connection with producing all the materials in their possession with respect to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. But you're, again, singling out the United States government, when the Prosecution has made it clear that we're not talking of any one particular country, but possibly of multiple countries. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, and let's finish it, please. Let's bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. Mr. Ostojic now brings the discussion to aerial imagery, and that's different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're not dealing with aerial imagery here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just responding to that argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. McCloskey, before we proceed any further, particularly before we proceed with any kind of decision, we would like to know from you the following: You've identified one country, that being Croatia, in respect of which there are no Rule 70 restrictions. We're only talking of possible intercepts. Is there any other country that has imposed the Rule 70 embargo in respect both -- or has asked for Rule 70 application, both in respect of the fact that they may have received a request from you for such information, from you, I say the Office of the Prosecutor, or that they may have supplied such information or has not supplied such information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just -- just to clear up Croatia briefly, they have provided us a body of intercepts which we have provided the Defence, and there's been testimony on them. The actual workings of how those intercepts were taken and all is currently part of another investigative team, and they're dealing with, I think, some issues along this line. But as for the body of Croatian intercepts that are out there, yeah, that's -- that's not Rule 70. There are other countries. There are multiple countries involved in requests of these kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you invoking the Rule 70 in respect of each and every one of these other countries?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As was expected when requests of this nature are made, they're made under Rule 70 and they don't go -- you know, we never get involved in the -- in the requests, nor of course the responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any other country that has not put Rule 70 condition in relation to intercept, other than Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to suggest that there's any countries that have even, because that's really not appropriate. But as for countries -- well, we had the RS and there's some intercepts from the RS, very few, but there's never -- there's been lots of requests, but I don't think they're saying or I've never heard them say Rule 70 in response to that. That's a little more complicated issue. But -- I'm sorry, let me look again at your question, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is what Judge Kwon -- or I was going to say "Mr. Justice," because that's what I'm used to. What Judge Kwon highlights, very simply put, is the following: You may have, when approaching these countries yourself, indicated Rule 70 privilege. What he is suggesting is that, however, in providing you with information or material, these countries may not have insisted on Rule 70 privileges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other -- any other information relating to intercepts that's out there in a non-Rule 70 world. None, not right now, and I'm trying to think if I'm missing something, but, no. Just that there's a few references to the RS, there's one intercept we picked up in the Bratunac Brigade that had to do with Naser Oric and Halilovic in 1992, which the Defence should have. But other intercepts out there or intercept information, I can't think of anything right now, but I'll continue to think. I can't think of anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the conditions of Rule 70 are such that whether the country has been asked itself, the fact should not arise in the course of trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, I was thinking about that question as well. Perhaps the question to test the Prosecution's -- well, have we done our homework, "Have you gone and asked for information out there in the Rule 70 world," I think that's probably, by itself, a fair question to test our ability or to test whether or not we've done what we should do. But anything, any inference related to that, aside from whether we've done proper investigative work, I don't think should be allowed; for example, who we ask such a question to, anything that would cause an inference that a country did or did not have it, answered or did not answer. Because, of course, if we'd ask a particular country, someone may infer that we knew something about that country that led us to believe they had that information, which -- so in the intelligence world, the question is sometimes as important, if not more so, than the answer. So the question, the broad question, "Have you gone besides your own investigation, you know, and asked outwardly," I think to test whether we've done a proper job, is okay. So, in that respect, I would pull back a bit from my more definitive position, but it needs to be general. It shouldn't be directed to one country or another, because inferences should not be drawn in that context, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go back a little bit in time to page 39. There were two questions put by Mr. Ostojic. One was a generic one, which has been answered and which we would have allowed, anyway: "Did you, sir, at any time review or request intercepts that may have been received from other countries or taken by other countries for the period in July of 1995?" The witness answered: "I am aware that the investigative team did request that information, sir." Then it's the second question that we will not allow: "Can you list for me the countries that they requested that information from?" Our decision is that the witness, because of Rule 70 restrictions that have been indicated by Mr. McCloskey, should not be in a position to identify countries that may have been asked or provided or not provided such information. I need to discuss one further point with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We also decide, I just wanted to make it clear, that we are unanimous on this, that as a follow-up to Mr. Ostojic's first question and the witness's answer, namely, that: "I am aware that the investigative team did request that information, yes, sir," it's perfectly legitimate for Mr. Ostojic to put a further question, namely: "Does that mean that you had at your disposal other intercepts from other countries?" The witness can answer that question, but the matter stops there. You cannot proceed any further with asking questions which would tend to identify one or more of these countries that we have the assurance of the OTP are covered by Rule-- or information which is covered under Rule 70 protection. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you perhaps explain that to Mr. Butler so it's clear to him? He knows about the Croatian intercepts and will probably want to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably, if there were others, he knows about theirs as well. Okay. All right. I will, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think he knows about the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's bring Mr. Butler back in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day, you would have had more breaks than we have. You were asked a question by Mr. Ostojic some minutes ago, which was the following: "Did you, sir, at any time review or request intercepts that may have been received from other countries or taken by other countries for the period in July of 1995?" To which you answered: "I am aware that the investigative team did request that information, yes, sir." You did not answer whether, in fact -- you did not state whether, in fact, you had at your disposal and reviewed and consulted other intercepts possibly provided from or by other countries. So if you are asked that question, you are requested to answer it, whether you did consult other intercepts from other countries. However, if you are asked to give an indication or to list which are these other countries that provided such intercepts, with the exception of Croatia, you're not allowed, you're not permitted to mention or identify any other country. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll put the question the Court permits. Did you -- first let me ask you this: You mentioned that the investigative team requested that information, and certainly you were part of that team; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who, in particular, requested that information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was all bundled into the request and done so under the direction of Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, the investigation team commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll talk about the commander in a little bit, but did you have at your disposal, in order to review, these other intercepts from other countries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I never had that material at my disposal at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we were discussing the material that you haven't received or reviewed, which would, for lack of a better term, as you put it, create some bias in your report. We covered the intercepts for now, and we'll come back to them. What about the documents from the ABiH Army? Did you obtain and review all the documents with respect to the ABiH military from July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I did not do a comprehensive review of all of the documents from the ABiH Army. The -- we did review, for the month of July, material that we were able to obtain in a subsequent search of 2 Corps that the Office of the Prosecutor did, as well as some ABiH Army documents that the VRS Zvornik Brigade had by virtue of their capture of the 28th Infantry Division records at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you review any records from the ABiH Army in connection with the period of July 1995 to determine their strategic, operational, or tactical orders from the ABiH Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. From the context of the documents that I just described, that was one of the reasons why I did look at them, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, sir, if you reviewed documents which would reveal the military strength of the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe some of those documents did give either in broad terms or actually troop lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was the number that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, off the top of my head, what the end strength was for the 28th Infantry Division from those documents. You probably could refresh my memory, but I just don't recall offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the weapons that were smuggled into Srebrenica in 1995? Did you get a comprehensive list or data from the ABiH Army with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material and my understanding of that is again from the documents that we've discussed. Investigatively, we didn't go to the ABiH and ask for a laundry list accounting of that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject, and that's aerial photographs. We discussed it briefly with Mr. Ruez, your commander, as you put it. Did you receive aerial -- or did you request and receive aerial photographs as to how many Muslim soldiers or combatants made it to Tuzla in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever request --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you're going to get that, but okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me your understanding of what an aerial photograph is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overhead aerial imagery, that's either taken from what we call air-breather platforms, which would be aircraft, or non-air-breathing platforms, which is satellite imagery.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is that done on a continuous basis, do you know, in July of 1995, or was that done sporadically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That is covered by Rule 70, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, help me with this: Did you analyse the aerial photographs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overhead imagery that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, I did, in fact, look at and used it as a component of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll call it an overhead imagery, if you'd like, although we were asked to call it, I thought, an aerial photograph. But just so we understand from looking at the transcript, that we're talking about the same thing. This overhead imagery that you looked at, was that given to you in hard copy or on disc or CD?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was provided to us hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, was anyone able, including Mr. Ruez, to remove any of the data that was on this hard copy of this aerial photograph or overhead imagery that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was possible, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why wouldn't it be possible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- well, I mean, for the same reasons, you know, on any hard copy product, if you start trying to modify or change a hard copy imagery product, like a photograph, there's going to be, you know, presumably noticeable marks on that. You know, I guess there's, you know, with newer technology, obviously the possibility of scanning hard copy and making a digital copy, doing the Photoshop and then spitting it out that way. But, I mean, to my knowledge, the substance of the images were not altered by Mr. Ruez for any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, do you remember if these overhead imageries that you reviewed, whether they had the symbol from NIMA, which is the National Imaging and Mapping Agency of the United States?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether they had them on the original hard copies that were provided under Rule 70 or not. They may have. I just don't recall at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Each and every one of them would have had it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each and every hard copy was labelled with respect to basic information as to what the title of the image was, as well as with respect to which direction north was so we could orient it. I remember a stamp saying, "Property of the United States Government, Rule 70," but I can't recall at this juncture whether a particular image had a particular agency reference on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what about dates? Did they have dates that were in a block that were on the overhead imagery at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, on the original overhead imagery, it did give us a date block, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did it give you a description of what it is that is purportedly reflected in the imagery?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original Rule 70 ones, there was an analyst description, one or two lines, as to what the analyst believed the -- a particular part of the image described.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to go back -- and we'll come back to the aerial imagery a little later, but I just want to cover this other material that perhaps was not in your possession or you didn't review. How about documents from the Main Staff? Do you, sir, think that you got a complete list of all the documents from the Main Staff? The reason I ask you that, just to put it in context: On January 16th, 2008, well, during your testimony here on page 11 through 12, you stated that you don't recall if you have any records relating to the Main Staff duty officer. So my question to you is: Did you obtain a comprehensive group of documents from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that the OTP has ever obtained a comprehensive list of documents from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if at any time you reviewed a vehicle log or vehicle logs from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever endeavour to search and obtain such information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did; and, in fact, that was the genesis of a future OTP search at the RS Ministry of Defence. As part of that search, we also talked to individuals who allegedly had information about Main Staff related documents, and those particular individuals were not able to tell us where the Main Staff archives, as we used to call them, were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you never obtained them; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, we still do not have a comprehensive collection of material that we call the Main Staff archives, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear the interpreters asking you to pause between question and answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Rather clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you also state, in your prior testimony and I think here during your testimony in this case, that you also don't, as a general rule, cite or attribute substantive information to witness interviews. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the reason you don't is because you're being brought here as an analyst for the OTP to provide context behind the documents and the intercepts, not to pass value judgements as to whether or not you believe or don't believe a witness and whether you can corroborate or not corroborate such witness's testimony. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that's the -- the complete accurate of what I'm trying to say behind this. My view is: It's not my job, with respect to these proceedings, to comment as to whether or not a particular witness is accurate or is not accurate or is complete. As an analyst, my ability to make a determination as to the full truthfulness of an individual who's given a witness statement is limited, particularly in the more advanced stages of our analysis, when, you know, there was an understanding that we would be going into court in the General Krstic case. You know, as a matter of practice, I didn't want to be in a position where I was relying for substantive issues on statements of individuals who I was aware that the Office of the Prosecutor was going to call as a witness and that, in that context, you know, the Court would make the determination as to the information and to the usefulness or veracity of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And let me just try to end before the break, if it's still at the same time. You know, people have called you a military expert, an intelligence analyst; but the truth of the matter, isn't it, Mr. Butler, that the report that you're giving here today and that you gave is more of as a historical analyst, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the particular context of the crime scene that we are working, yes, it is a historical analytical report. I am not being asked to do predictive analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In respect of the rest --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I wasn't looking at Mr. President. Was that directed to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It was directed to Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm asking is and the question was: "Isn't it correct, Mr. Butler, that the report you're giving here today and that you gave is more of a historical analyst, is it not?" Then you said: "In the particular context of the crime scene that we are working, yes, it is a historical and analytical report. I'm not being asked to do predictive analysis." In respect to other sectors of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. My report obviously deals with a fixed point in time, either with respect to the crime base of July of 1995; or, with respect to the command reports, the past practices and rules and regulations of the VRS as they were applied in July of 1995. In that context, they're historical. However, as I've noted in the context of my very first report, it's not designed to be a historical overview. There are many political, there are many military, there are many diplomatic issues that are obviously related to these things that are beyond my ability to analyse and intelligently comment on. So, in that respect, you know, I go back to the original purposes of my report, which were to set the framework for the military context and how they related to the crime bases that were being investigated, with respect to the actual linkage of military units to crime scenes and the actual roles and responsibilities of individuals designated as commanders or other members of those units with respect to their roles and responsibilities under the VRS rules as they applied. By design, that is where I limited my analytical focus to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear enough. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you, before we go on this break, with respect to Rule 68, are you familiar with that rule?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were familiar with it when you were working for the OTP for those six years; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, beyond even my own analytical practices of keeping other options open, particularly as we got into the situation where individuals were indicted and subsequently apprehended, and particularly in the case of General Krstic, where he was interviewed and did articulate some of these various other -- I don't want to say -- I mean, in short, the fact -- yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the fact that we held that open, those possibilities open, specifically because that was part of meeting our Rule 68 obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just talking about you right now. We'll come back to Mr. Ruez and other people on this investigative team. But is it true that in the Krstic case, you were primarily used by the OTP as a vehicle to provide information that was believed to be Rule 68 in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so my learned friends have the cite, November 17, 2003, page 4717.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that during the Krstic case, that there were times that I did testify about material that was deemed to be Rule 68, and my presence in the courtroom made it a mechanism to do that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you the person who's in charge and used as a vehicle to provide information which was believed to be Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in charge of Rule 68, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was on your investigative team while you were there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lawyers collectively were the ultimate arbitrators of whether or not information was Rule 68. The analysts and the investigators, when they recognised information that might fall into that category, we brought it to the trial attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was the mode of communication that you brought it to the trial attorneys; written, oral, or any other type?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, I would park in their office and explain it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you would not keep a memo of it or record contemporaneously that you thought document X, Y, and Z may potentially be Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those discussions that may exist would be relevant to e-mails --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- yes. So, I mean, there are, I'm sure, written references to it. I know, from my own purposes, there were notes and everything else that I would be keeping; and if there were issues that I believed -- or discussions on Rule 68, I would note that. So, certainly, notes do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's from every member of the team; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for every member of the team. I can only speak for the military analysts who were working for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, you yourself, ever assemble or gather materials that may be deemed Rule 68 for any of the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, with respect to Colonel Pandurevic, yes, simply because he was someone who we had indicted early on. After leaving the OTP, my ability to do that, you know, to rifle through document collections and things of that nature, was considerably more limited. So I can't say that I specifically went through the volume collections looking for Rule 68 information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many military analysts were there with the OTP on this investigative team that was led by Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself; my partner, Ms. Amanda Brettell; my research assistant or our research assistant, Ms. Sally Lattin; and a group of either translators or language assistants who would rotate through.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who in that group was in charge of gathering materials that may be deemed Rule 68 for Mr. Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I mean, my understanding, in the case of Beara, was that I was gone by that time, so I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we continue after the break, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the dates that may appear on these various images? Was that ever altered or erased by Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The dates, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. I wouldn't expect it to be, because that would even - we can agree on this, I'm sure - that would be not only unethical. It would be wrong, biased, and it would be something that is not comprehensible; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, I mean, you know, there were issues where we went through and tried to determine better times and everything else; but I'm not aware that on US government imagery, that a date was arbitrarily changed by the Office of the Prosecutor to reflect what day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about erased?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the imagery products look like in this trial, so I don't know whether they were erased or not. I mean, I know that in previous trials, as a practice, we did not erase dates. When we made products for court, we asked for the unannotated versions from the US government, and then the dates were put on by the Office of the Prosecutor. They reflected the same dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But to change or alter or to erase dates, to answer the question that I posed earlier, would you consider that to be unethical?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This was dealt with Mr. Ruez, the person that was involved with this, and that's the appropriate place to deal with it, not to -- not having Mr. Butler speculate on products that were made for this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness has already agreed with Mr. Ostojic in any case, so let's move to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look, if you don't mind, on Exhibit P02103, which is a photo book that was used and provided by Mr. Ruez in his testimony of the 18th of September, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'd like us to look at image number 236, if we can. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Great. Now, you see the emblem on the box in the centre of the image on the left side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's from NIMA; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little small, but I'll take your word for it. If you want to blow it up, I can confirm it, but I don't believe it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it is, but we can confirm it if you have any doubt.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, did every -- since you received these aerial images in hard copy, to the best of your recollection, did every aerial photograph or imagery contained this emblem?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the material provided by the US government for the -- part of the investigation, I don't recall whether it did or not. No, sir, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did it include the little box right under the emblem with the date or was that something that was placed there by the Office of the Prosecution and their investigative team?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The captions that are encircled in white are placed by the United States government. Any annotations to the image, at least was the policy that -- when I was here, annotations to the image in yellow are those that are placed by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with the white box on the lower right-hand side, where I believe it's, "February 1st, 2000," or maybe I'm misreading it. But it has some digital numbers and then it has the "1" and then space, two zeros, and then "FEB." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Having worked with the United States military, can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That particular sequence number is not a number that is normally associated with products like this. I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what sequence -- what sequence numbers would be associated with products like these if this is isn't one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we've gone far enough into something he doesn't know, and this is obviously trying to break the veil of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just be heard briefly, and I know we probably -- I've probably exhausted your patience on this, and I apologise. These were the very same questions we asked of Mr. Ruez on the 14th of September, 2006, and I can give you the page cite. They objected and said, "We'll wait," and the Court said, "We'll wait and we can get those answers when there's a US government attorney here." So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But independent and irrespective of all that, the witness has told you he hasn't got a clue. So if he hasn't got a clue, what that means, how can you proceed with your next question, the one that you put? Mr. McCloskey is right. I mean, you can't ask a second question when the witness has told you, "I haven't got a clue."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think if we read his answer -- I won't debate it with the Court. I'll just move on, but we may come back to it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we now look, sir, at, in this same group of exhibits, P02103, Exhibit 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just to help, it should be the Bratunac city, Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the pages might be off by one, as we've learned during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it what you were looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. President. The very next one, I think, and they're getting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the right one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you, Madam Usher and Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, just for the record, that it's "123"? Would that be correct? "121", you're right. "121", just so we have a clean record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is another aerial image. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in this aerial image, the NIMA emblem does not appear; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the digitalised information that we saw in the prior exhibit, 236, on the lower right-hand corner does not appear as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Those kinds of questions are not authorised by the United States, as far as I know. How things are made, why things like that are on the net is an area that I'm fairly clear is something that is not part of the Rule 70 clearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, do you want to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MS. SCHILDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We just need a confirmation or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SCHILDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I am not exactly -- excuse me. I'm not certain where counsel is going with this, but I think we have been quite clear with the Court and the Defence counsel as to the conditions under which the images were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor and authorised for use in court under Rule 70. I think we submitted two letters to Mr. McCloskey on November 3rd, 2006 and August 13th, 2007, that explained how we provided the images. The process of what the Office of the Prosecutor did with those images after they were provided, we did make clear, in a letter that we authorised Mr. McCloskey to share with the Court, that the OTP was authorised to use the imagery to produce materials for use in court, including applying markings that would be clearly distinguishable from the original US government markings. However, we are not or the United States is not in a position to provide any further information about these images. They were provided under Rule 70. I think we have been quite forthcoming about the process by which we provided them. I also do not believe Mr. Butler would be in a position to speak to the US process for providing these images and authorising them for use in court. I understand he was working with the OTP, so he may be in a position to speak to the OTP process for dealing with them, but certainly not with the US government side of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SCHILDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Shall I continue? I guess not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once more, we are fine tuned, and this is a unanimous decision: You pointed out, Mr. Ostojic, to the witness, and actually asked him: "And the digitalised information that we saw on the prior 236 on the lower right-hand corner does not appear as well?" In this one, I mean one-to-one. He answered: "Yes." Then you asked him: "How is that?" That is not the kind of question that we can allow. You can rephrase it in the sense of asking the witness whether the Office of the Prosecutor did any alterations on one-to-one to the extent of removing any such digitalised information that shows in other exhibits, like Exhibit 236. Am I clear or do you want a further explanation? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness has understood what I said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, my learned friend from the US government said that the OTP was instructed that they can apply markings, but, sir, I'm really focusing on eraser of markings from documents given to the OTP by the United States in their original form. The Court put that question to you, sir: Was there anything erased by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not involved with the process of imagery with respect to the presentation or anything of that nature. I can't tell you what happened, why it happened, or what the motivations were. So, I mean, the short answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, help me with this. Who would know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. Ruez has spoken specifically to this issue. I don't know if anyone remembers it, but it was a long time ago, and we're getting pretty far afield with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, again I have to go back; and if the Court looks at the testimony, we were prohibited from asking Mr. Ruez these very questions, Your Honour, specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you answer the question that has been put to you by Mr. Ostojic, in any case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I was out of the Office of the Prosecutor in November of 2004. I have no idea what might or might have transpired post that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's move to your next question, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the requests that were made for these aerial images, do you know if they were date-specific or were they general requests?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial collection of aerial images that were provided to the OTP were already here before I had arrived. I don't know the genesis of the request behind that. I know that when we came across a specific piece of information with respect to the investigation, that we felt, for example -- you know, something obvious that we felt that maybe there could be assistance on, like a mass grave or a particular location, we would ask for imagery product of a specific geographic area. What the United States government or what anyone else provided, and the dates surrounding that, were outside our control. We didn't go by date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Looking at this exhibit from P02103, number 121, do you see the box immediately below the word "Bratunac" on the top left-hand or near the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is that a box, to the best of your knowledge, that contained a date at some time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of my knowledge, it's a box. I have no way of being able to tell you what was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You don't know if, in that box, there was a date and a time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As an analyst, did you ever see or do you know why your investigative team would remove dates from the box, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. Mr. Ostojic, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this, with your logic, if you will, Mr. Butler. If a date can be removed from a box such as this on 121, it can be also replaced with a different date and time, can it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The same objection. This issue has been dealt with by Mr. Ruez. He was allowed to ask questions and answer questions on that. Now he's bringing Mr. Butler in just to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Butler can only speculate, having already stated that he doesn't know what could and what couldn't be done. He's also explained to you that maybe if there is a scanning and a reproduction of a hard copy, then one can play around, but that's as far as he could get. So your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's our position that not only were the dates in the boxes able to be manipulated or erased, but also the data that's contained in the center larger box that you see from members of the investigative team. My question to you is, sir: Do you know if the investigative team had that capacity to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea whether they would have or not after my departure. I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: Do you know if they had the capacity to do it, sir, the technical wherewithal to do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. We've talked about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, we are just in a purely speculative mode here. So let's move, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He didn't answer my question. He answered it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To us, a question asked and answered. So let's move to the next question, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, my learned friend at the Office of the Prosecution said that you're kind of an expert or an analyst with respect to documents and that you could really kind of -- when you look at something like, for example, an intercept, that you can determine whether or not it's authentic, or reliable, and things of that sort. Do you remember giving that testimony in your direct examination on January 14th, 2008?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that -- I don't think I ever said I could look at an intercept and determine whether it's authentic and the source of a document expert. So I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the sake of time, you are not a document expert; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a forensic/technical sense, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In any sense, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My expertise is the ability to look at the documents and to determine what they mean contextually on the basis of this crime scene. That's it; that's all I advertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you can't tell, by looking at either the aerial images or the intercept, whether or not those documents, from a forensic standpoint, have been altered, modified, changed; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't look at a particular image and tell you, with any degree of reliability, whether it's been altered, doctored, changed, or otherwise. No, sir. It's not my technical field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in trying to give us this objective review, historically, that you're analysing for us, wouldn't that be something that you would consider in your purported analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the national providers of these images might have altered the information in order to make it appear as other things?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For example, if members of the investigative team that you worked with did that, would that be helpful for you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It clarifies it, but, no, I did not consider the fact that for the use of my analysis and what I used the images for, that that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with Mr. Ruez or inquire about this empty box or the ability to remove things from a box on an aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not spoken with Mr. Ruez for the better part of two years, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that means that you have not talked to him at all while you were here, up until November 2004, and subsequent to that, up to the last two years that you've spoken to him, about these empty boxes and the ability of the OTP to alter or change them; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the intercepts for a moment. You mentioned them in some of your reports. You didn't obtain any information as to whether or not any of the intercepts that you reviewed were modified, altered, or changed in any way; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By members, I assume, of the investigative team, as opposed to the provider of the material?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can start there.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, which one is "there"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The investigative team.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I received no information from members of the investigative team that they were deliberately altering the content of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about from the provider, the Bosnian Muslim intercept operators, did you obtain any such information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- as part of the authentication process, when there were questions as to whether or not there were discrepancies between the versions that were what we call the printout versions or the handwritten versions, I understand that the investigative team and Ms. Frease and her people went out and resolved them. So we knew that there were always going to be minor discrepancies. We've had numbers of occasions where two or three different intercepts appear for the same date and there are discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, how would you define a major discrepancy? Being this analyst, what would constitute a major discrepancy to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A major discrepancy with the -- with the intent of an intercept would be, for example, where we would have two or three versions of the same intercept and that not only would there be missing gaps, which could be explained by an intercept site not having access to the full component of the transmission, but would be an entirely different context of the discussion. So, in that context, that's what I would call a major discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you also call a major discrepancy if a letter identifying, purportedly, one of the participants was changed or modified on a couple of occasions, so that it would be a different initial or different initials as opposed to the one in its original form?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the names, in Serbo-Croatian, the same last name can be pronounced or even spelled a little bit differently for cultural or parentage reasons, but I'm not aware of a situation where initials that are attributed to correspondence are being arbitrarily changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. That information is something that you've never come across; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have come across it, but I'm not aware of a situation that's standing out at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And it's certainly not included in any of your reports, is it, that you said: "Well, this intercept may not be as reliable or authentic because the provider altered or modified, on a couple of occasions, the identity of the purported speaker"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the short version is if I believe that that was the case, it wouldn't be in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It would not be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I believe that that was the case, it would not be in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That analysis or that intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That intercept. I wouldn't reference it and I would not count on it for any particular reason if the origins -- if I understood that the origins were questionable or if there had been a deliberate attempt to alter it or modify it for the purpose of changing my analysis or steering me somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that would be Rule 68 material, would it not, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that misconduct on the part of the Office of the Prosecutor would qualify as Rule 68 if it were done by the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're speaking of the provider, with all due respect now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that if the investigative team had information that providers had altered it, that it would fall under the rubric of Rule 68, because it would call into question parts of the authenticity process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I just want to cover a couple more aerial images, and then we'll move from this topic for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be if you'd look at aerial image I believe it's 249, if we have the correct numbering system.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have that image now in front of you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just to make sure I have my complete record on this, we know there's no emblem there and nothing on the lower right-hand side that's digitalised. There's not even an empty box underneath the broader box identifying the area purportedly; is that correct? You don't see a blank box there, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't see a blank box.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know how, in this specific aerial image, there is no date that's below the description? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's asking him to speculate on the provider in this particular area, and that's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Necessarily, I think he either knows or he doesn't. If he doesn't, we move. If he's in a position to give us information related to OTP only, not to the US government, then I think you can safely proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is, no, I have no idea why there or is not one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look, if we may, at - and I thank you for your patience, Your Honour, on this, and the Registry and the Usher - Exhibit 27 of this collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have that in front of you, do you not, sir, this image 27, which is of purportedly a bus convoy at Nova Kasaba? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the box below that has both the date and what seems to be the time. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, looking at now these four or five pictures, why they're different, in the sense that some pictures have the emblem, some don't; others have a box which is empty, some have only the date, and some have the date and the time on the specific photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As that material is referenced to the black and white, that's US material, and why it's on one and not on the another, is not appropriate. He can ask him all day long about the yellow markings. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I don't know that Mr. McCloskey is here testifying that the black and white is necessarily US material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He doesn't have to specify on that. If he makes a statement, that's enough. If he makes a statement to that effect, and I think we have heard it also from Mr. Ruez, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is part of the explanation we gave way back when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not testimony. So let's move to your next question. And in any case, it's a question which has been already put and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll have to look at the transcript for that, Your Honour, but thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, being a historical analyst, let me ask you: How many reports did you generate with respect to the Srebrenica issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first report was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just give me the number, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think related to Srebrenica, a total of five.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And one was the brigade command structure; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one was the corps command report; one was the brigade command report; the original version of the Srebrenica military narrative; the revised version of that, which came out several -- well, two years later; and, most recently, the Main Staff report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that when you describe yourself as a historical analyst, that that would really be what the two Srebrenica narrative reports are? They are simply your historical analysis of the events; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. We've been through this. This is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least in relation to what he is testifying and the report that we have in this case, it has certainly been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll look to the transcript for your guidance on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He also specified which part of the report he considers to be historical, a historical account. I put a question in addition to yours, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I was following up, but we'll look at it again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to your testimony on the 14th of January, 2008, on the military prosecutor's office, on page I think it's 19607, you state the following - and just in the moments that we have here, I want to get a better understanding- you state, "In 1992, at the time this memorandum was published..." I think we're referencing 65 ter 28, and that was what I added to your statement. "In 1992, at the time this memorandum was published, the military prosecutor's office, the military court system, were under the administration of the VRS. At a later point in the war, those responsibilities were relinquished by the army and, in fact, picked up by the Ministry of Defence." Do you remember giving that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't know if I used the phrase -- if I used the phrase "relinquished." It's more accurately they were transferred. But yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was just quoting you verbatim, but that's fair if you want to use the word" transfer." Help me with this: When was it exactly this period that you refer to at a later point in the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If memory serves, it was sometime either in late 1993, early 1994. It was after the Banja Luka mutinies. I know that there is a considerable amount of documents related to that. It's hopefully somewhere in a binder where my desk used to be, but I can't tell you exactly, offhand, what the date is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You had a group of binders with you here last week, and I did notice you don't have them this week. Are those binders available to you to bring tomorrow, so that we could see specifically the rule or the reference that you made, that in 1993 and 1994, these responsibilities were transferred and/or relinquished by the VRS to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material won't be in those binders, because those are only the exhibits that were tendered or asked by the Prosecutor for me. I don't think that that was an issue that was one that was going to be tendered through exhibits or anything else like that, so I don't think that there's going to be a document that says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the minute or two or three that we have, can you identify the document more precisely for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be - and I'm reaching back on this one - some form of either a Main Staff directive that notes that or an Official Gazette directive that talks about the military prosecutor's office, under the Ministry of Defence, as opposed to the army. I mean, I know the information's out there, but I'm just drudging back through old memory on that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, Mr. McCloskey, can you reach a stipulation on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure we can, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it takes two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're always willing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It takes two to tango.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will look for the documents. It's not something I recall off the top of my head, either, but I know there's documents that Mr. Butler is referencing, and we can start looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can break now for the day, Your Honour, I'm about to go on to another subject area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Butler, thank you so much. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just logistically, Mr. President, while it's always hard to tell how long Mr. Butler will go, but if we go with the estimates, he's going to run out of cross-examination at our deadline date, and we still have Mr. Vasic, these DNA people, and one other short witness that you had approved. So we need some planning guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we're thinking about that, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If it please the Court, I'd just like the Chamber to know that we are attempting to reach a stipulation which would allow the Prosecutor not to have to call Mr. Vasic. We don't know if we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
